newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lawyer hails release of Russian ex-officer.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer hails release of Russian ex-officer.

text.p: The release of a retired navy captain jailed for nearly a year on suspicion of revealing Russian state secrets to an environmental group marks a historic victory for human rights, his lawyer said on Sunday.

"This is the first case in the history of Soviet-Russian state security that social pressure has succeeded in forcing the Federal Security Service (FSB) to observe the laws and stop its trampling of human rights," Yuri Schmidt said in a statement.
The FSB is the successor organisation of the notorious Soviet-era KGB secret police.
Schmidt said he was confident the charge of treason, which still stands, would eventually be dropped against his client Alexander Nikitin, who was released on Saturday.

"We are confident that the Nikitin case will be stopped. There has been no such case since Soviet times," said the statement, distributed during a news conference given by Schmidt in Nikitin's home city of St Petersburg.

Dubbed Russia's first post-communist political prisoner by international human rights groups, Nikitin was freed after the intervention of the deputy chief prosecutor Mikhail Katushev and members of the Russian parliament, Schmidt said.

Nikitin is now suffering from acute exhaustion and his eyesight has also been impaired after being cooped up in a small cell without natural light for 10 months, his wife Tatyana Chernova told the same news conference.

Nikitin fell foul of the authorities after writing about the hazards posed by the nuclear submarines of Russia's Northern Fleet in a report published earlier this year by Norway's Bellona environmental organisation.
He was arrested in February but formal charges were not brought until October, a year after the FSB raided Bellona's offices in the Arctic port of Murmansk.

It confiscated computers, data discs and other material and said later some of them contained state secrets, an allegation denied by Bellona, which is carrying out research into the risks of the ageing fleet on Norway's doorstep.
The FSB said in October Nikitin had been charged on three counts -- treason, revealing state secrets and forgery.
FSB sources said Nikitin continued to use his military identification card to gain access to top secret documents on Bellona's behalf after he was retired from active service.

A Bellona spokeswoman told Reuters on Saturday that Nikitin had spoken to the organisation since his release and had said he looked forward to resuming his work to contain radioactive pollution on the Kola peninsula.

Interfax news agency quoted Schmidt as saying an additional investigation into the Nikitin case would be carried out by independent experts. Until his name was finally cleared, Nikitin would not be allowed to leave St Petersburg, Interfax said.

"I am convinced that this affair will be halted without a trial, not right now but a little later," Schmidt said, adding that the FSB would try to think up some excuse for keeping Nikitin in detention rather than admit to making a mistake.
